Until recently, China was an important excep-
tion among low-income countries. There, between
1960 and 1980, state enterprises provided health
care directly to their workers or contracted with
government hospitals to do so. Rural communes
were required to earmark a portion of their finan-
cial resources for health services for all their mem-
bers. By the late 1970s insurance covered virtually
all the urban population and 85 percent of the rural
populationa unique achievement for a low-
income developing country. Since the elimination
of communal agriculture and the liberalization of
industry in the early 1980s, however, these forms
of health insurance and service delivery have
